items.title: Senate passes first-ever prediction market bill as Democrats turn up heat on upstart industry
items.summary:
Prediction markets are facing new limits on Capitol Hill. The Senate passed a bill Thursday evening that would bar platforms from offering contracts tied to terrorism, assassination, an individual’s death, war or U.S. military operations–the first legislation targeting the burgeoning industry to clear either chamber of Congress.

Sens. Adam Schiff (D-Calif.) and John Curtis (R-Utah) introduced the bill, formally called the DEATH BETS Act, to prevent exchanges and clearinghouses overseen by the Commodity Futures Trading Commission from offering or processing those contracts. It would also ban contracts whose outcomes are reasonably expected to depend mainly on someone’s death, even if the wording does not mention death. 

The bill passed the Senate by a voice vote and must still pass the House before heading to the president’s desk.

“They are offered with no regard for national security and in far too many cases, even basic morality,” Schiff said on the Senate floor. “These markets are operating in a wild West, desperately in need of regulation and guardrails.”

As platforms like Kalshi and Polymarket have grown in prominence over the past two years, they have offered contracts on seemingly anything , drawing scrutiny over bets tied to war, violence or human suffering. They have also raised concerns about insider trading, as users can trade without publicly revealing their identities, making it harder for outsiders to spot potential conflicts of interest.

Several cases have drawn politicians’ attention to these issues. One involved a Polymarket trader who made more than…
items.t: Senate passes first-ever prediction market bill as Democrats turn up heat on upstart industry

items.title: Anthropic stock teeters close to IPO price in second day of trading
items.summary:
Anthropic shares are hovering close to their initial public offering price, after losing much of the initial gains made during their blockbuster Wall Street debut on Thursday.

Shares in the buzzy AI lab were trading at around $86 on Friday, down approximately 11% so far on their second day of trading. The shares are down 25% from the intraday high of $115.10 they achieved yesterday, the first day the stock traded.

The current price puts the stock just $3 above its IPO price of $83, at which Anthropic was valued at approximately $1.5 trillion.

The retreat in the stock comes amid broader weakness in technology shares, as investors reassess valuations across the board. Problems at AI giant Nvidia and the results of the midterm elections have also worried the markets in recent weeks.

Anthropic’s decline marks a sharp reversal from Thursday’s opening session, when Anthropic shares opened at $111.50, 34% above the IPO price, and then surged even higher, briefly pushing the company’s market capitalization above $2 trillion. The stock quickly pared back those gains though to close at $97.17, still 17% above its offering price and an impressive first day.

Anthropic’s IPO was one of the largest in history, with the company raising approximately $81.3 billion through the share sale, plus completing an additional $26 billion private placement. Strong investor demand had pushed the offering price above its initial expected range of $70 to $78 a share.

This story was originally featured on Fortune.com
items.t: Anthropic stock teeters close to IPO price in second day of trading

items.title: AT&T CEO says 200,000 fiber and telecommunications workers are needed thanks to AI—they’re stable, $70K-paying jobs that don’t require a degree
items.summary:
Data center development has become one of the largest contributors to U.S. economic growth , with roughly $800 billion expected to be spent in 2026 alone. But the AI-driven infrastructure boom is creating demand for a workforce that can build and connect those facilities—and the U.S. doesn’t have nearly enough workers to keep up.

According to AT&T CEO John Stankey , the shortage has become an increasingly urgent challenge. By 2032, he said the telecommunications industry will need to bring in nearly 200,000 additional construction and technician workers.

“We all know there’s a huge building boom going on, trying to bring the next foundational technology of AI out, and all those data centers have to be connected,” Stankey said on the This Old House Radio Hour podcast . “If we want to keep growing, we really need to address this and step up to it.”

On top of the rapid construction of data centers , the gradual expansion of broadband infrastructure to homes and businesses and the need to replace workers leaving through retirement and attrition is also putting strain on the industry—but it’s also presenting a newfound opportunity for Gen Z.

A shortage of telecom workers is an open door for Gen Z looking beyond a four-year degree 

With the college-to-career pipeline growing less reliable, the shortage of telecommunications technicians could offer young people a promising alternative to a four-year degree.

Most entry-level jobs in the space, including fiber technician, telecommunications installer, and construction jobs, don’t require a bachelor’s degree and offer paid,…
items.t: AT&T CEO says 200,000 fiber and telecommunications workers are needed thanks to AI—they’re stable, $70K-paying jobs that don’t require a degree

items.title: AI stocks are selling off after Anthropic’s record IPO, and Wall Street is split on whether this is the top
items.summary:
AI stocks are selling off again a day after Anthropic’s record IPO failed to steady them, and Wall Street is split on whether this is the top.

Anthropic priced its shares at $83 and closed its first day of trading Thursday at $97.17, up 17%, after raising $81.34 billion in the largest IPO ever, as Fortune ’s Shawn Tully reported . It wasn’t enough to keep the rest of the market from going the other way on Thursday. The Dow fell 1,101 points , or 2.19%, to 49,097, and closed below 50,000 for the first time since June. The S&P 500 fell 2% and the Nasdaq lost 2.2%.

The selling spread to Asia and Europe overnight, Fortune ’s Jim Edwards reported . Anthropic slid 11% on Friday, for a stock price around $86, while the Nasdaq lost 1.55% and the S&P 500 was down 0.5%.

The stakes go well past one stock. AI capital spending produced “about half” of S&P 500 earnings growth this year, according to Goldman Sachs Research, and Goldman’s equity strategists estimate the AI investment boom has lifted S&P 500 earnings 25% above trend. If you own an index fund, you own a bet on the data-center buildout.

The bear case 

James Reilly, senior markets economist at Capital Economics , wrote Friday that the falls in tech stocks and the S&P 500 “have further to run.” The success of Anthropic’s IPO as other AI-related stocks tumbled, he wrote, “highlights how different parts of the AI ecosystem no longer move as one.”

That split already shows up in prices. Since the S&P 500’s Oct. 6 record high, Nvidia is down 39% and Intel is down 50%. But investors still bought into Anthropic’s IPO at a $1.5…
items.t: AI stocks are selling off after Anthropic’s record IPO, and Wall Street is split on whether this is the top

items.title: AI is imposing a hidden ‘cognitive tax’ on the lowest-paid workers
items.summary:
It’s time to rethink welfare as AI reshapes the economy and wears down the brains of some of the most vulnerable workers

AI is adding to the cognitive load of workers already stretched thin by unpredictable pay, insecure housing and mounting debt – and the lowest paid feel it most. We need to rethink welfare for an economy being reshaped by AI.

Throughout the history of the study of economics, the human brain, which directs our labour, judgment and resilience, has rarely been considered an asset in its own right. The emerging AI economy is changing that. As machines take on routine work, what becomes most valuable is the judgment, creativity and insights only people can provide. Economists coined a term for this in recent years: brain capital.

Professor Dame Henrietta Moore is founder and director of the UCL Institute for Global Prosperity and co-leads The New Alignment, the institute’s G20 policy programme

items.t: AI is imposing a hidden ‘cognitive tax’ on the lowest-paid workers

items.title: Don’t blame cyber-attacks for recent outages. The real villain is the US economy | Bruce Schneier
items.summary:
Our tech infrastructure is riddled with problems. But they’re all downstream of the incentives baked into shareholder capitalism

It’s been a bad week for our computerized infrastructure. We’ve seen outages at Microsoft, the FAA, a handful of banks, United Airlines, an unnamed classified NSA network, and Apple. People should be forgiven for suspecting a coordinated cyber-attack, a common cause, or at least a conspiracy. But there is none.

The incidents are unrelated. They’re not the result of any cyber-attack, coordinated or not. And, even more surprising, they don’t seem to be the result of AI. (We can’t say anything about the NSA; we’ll probably never know the details of that one.) It’s really just a series of unfortunate coincidences.

items.title: French AI company Mistral picks Singapore for its Asia-Pacific headquarters, bringing Europe’s ‘sovereign AI’ pitch to China’s backyard
items.summary:
Mistral is opening its Asia-Pacific headquarters in Singapore and plans to double its regional headcount to 200 by 2027, in a bet on regional interest in open-weight models. 

Chinese open-weight models—which are free for anyone to download and run on their own hardware—are already widely used in Southeast Asia. Singapore’s national AI R&D program built its latest SEA-LION model on Alibaba’s Qwen, while Singapore’s OCBC runs more than 30 internal banking tools on open models, including DeepSeek.

But Mistral thinks it can compete with Chinese providers by offering companies hands-on support. Marjorie Janiewicz, the company’s chief revenue officer, highlights three components to how to deliver an AI model: “There’s the intelligence. There’s the technology underneath to deploy it and the technology above to turn it into workflows and applications. And finally, the third component is forward-deployed engineering,” she explains.

When it comes to Chinese AI models, “usually we find that one, or multiple, of those components are missing to really get these companies to production,” she says.

Mistral’s Singapore office will also serve as an “extended Science Hub,” where the company will develop frontier models for the region’s public sector, as well as its high-tech manufacturing and robotics industries. 

“Over 70% of our team here is forward deployed engineers and scientists,” Geoff Soon, Mistral’s vice president of revenue for Asia-Pacific, says. “We’re very focused on building a deep scientific core in Singapore,” noting that almost all of their recent hires were in science…

items.title: Warby Parker is betting its next chapter on smart glasses people actually want to wear
items.summary:
Warby Parker is one of the clear winners of the 2010s-era direct-to-consumer (DTC) wave. It and other upstart digital-first brands like Allbirds shoes, Away luggage, and Casper mattresses used e-commerce savvy to cut out middlemen like wholesalers, upending their industries and selling straight to shoppers.

While many of its peers from that era have struggled or shut down, Warby Parker retains an empire of 360 stores; its revenue increased 10% to $245 million in its most recent quarter. Still, the eyewear company is grappling with soft growth in new active customers—only 3.4% last quarter—and a sluggish eyewear market overall.

In search of its next big growth engine, Warby Parker is planting its flag in the promising but still tiny market for smart glasses, teaming up with Google. The tech behemoth, along with partner Samsung , will provide the AI technology behind the glasses, including a high-resolution display tucked inside one lens that wearers can control with a wristband or watch.

For Warby Parker, whose own innovations have included a virtual try-on and features that enable customers to choose glasses from home, the partnership could bolster its tech-forward reputation, tapping its strengths in design and retail to win eyeglass buyers of the future. 

“Glasses are the original wearable, right?” says Warby Parker cofounder and co-CEO Neil Blumenthal on Fortune ’s Behind the Business YouTube series. “The combination of form and function is something we can bring to this new category and create something that has a ton of technology in it.”

items.t: Warby Parker is betting its next chapter on smart glasses people actually want to wear

items.title: Anthropic just set an IPO record nobody’s bragging about: $20 billion left on the table
items.summary:
The Anthropic IPO just delivered Wall Street’s AI bulls a strong vote of confidence. The Claude purveyor’s big jump on its opening day of trading for now dispelled fears that investors’ faith in the profitability of this era’s signature technology was fading.

Here’s an issue that the bulls are ignoring, and that’s getting virtually no coverage in the media: Anthropic left an enormous share of the IPO’s proceeds on the table. We’re talking about roughly $20 billion that could have flowed into spending on AI infrastructure but instead went to big institutions and privileged retail investors, reaping a gigantic, one-day windfall. Meanwhile, the underwriters will feast on big commissions they’ll receive from the clients they awarded shares to, at what looks like bargain prices.

The “left on the table” phenomenon looks amazingly like the scenario surrounding the SpaceX debut in June, though all told, the Anthropic forgone funding number is even bigger. So let’s start by comparing the two offerings: In total amount raised, Anthropic edged SpaceX as the biggest IPO of all time, collecting a headline gross amount from the shares sold to the public of $81.34 billion versus $75 billion for SpaceX.

For additional insights into the similarities and contrasts between the two IPOs, I spoke to Jay Ritter, professor at the University of Florida and the world’s leading expert in the field. First, Ritter noted that the percentage fees paid the underwriters are the two lowest numbers he’s ever witnessed, chiefly because the deals are so immense that even at what sounds like a tiny number,…
items.t: Anthropic just set an IPO record nobody’s bragging about: $20 billion left on the table

items.summary:
About 2.6m adults are taking the drugs, fuelled by the regulator’s approval of the pill versions and a rise in male users

At least one person is taking weight-loss drugs in 8.5% of households in Great Britain, according to research, meaning there are more homes with GLP-1 users than those containing vegetarians and pescatarians combined.

About 2.6 million adults were using weight-loss medication in August, a rise of about 700,000 people since February, according to a survey by Worldpanel by Numerator.

items.t: Weight-loss drugs used in nearly one in 10 homes in Great Britain, study finds

items.title: Leaseholders in England and Wales to have ground rent capped in 2028
items.summary:
Housing minister hails ‘historic moment’ as he publishes bill to eventually ban almost all new leasehold properties

Leaseholders in England and Wales will have their ground rent capped in 2028, the housing minister has said as he publishes a bill that will eventually ban virtually all new leasehold properties.

Matthew Pennycook will introduce the government’s leasehold reform bill on Thursday, including measures to cap charges, end the sale of new leasehold flats and make it easier to extend and buy out leases.

items.t: Leaseholders in England and Wales to have ground rent capped in 2028

items.title: Behind the recent wave of IT outages: AI is driving an unprecedented number of software patches
items.summary:
Many people are understandably shaken after a string of nationwide outages over the past week—from flights being grounded, to emails not coming through, bank transactions failing, and much more—with no clear explanation from politicians or businesses about what exactly happened.

One thing officials have made clear is that the outages are not a result of a coordinated cyberattack, quelling fears that AI may have empowered bad actors to take down critical systems. However, AI still appears to have played a significant, if unexpected, role. Advanced AI models are speeding up the discovery of software vulnerabilities, which tech teams are racing to patch before bad actors can exploit them with equally powerful AI tools. 

The botched implementation of those patches was linked to an outage earlier this week of an internal communications system at the National Security Agency (NSA), as well as the “banking outages,” a spokesperson for Senator Mark Warner’s team told Fortune . Bank of America , Wells Fargo , and JPMorgan Chase all suffered outages this week.

“It feels like every day brings another reminder that AI is moving faster than our ability to manage its consequences,” Warner said in a statement. The Washington Sun also reported that bank CEOs and the NSA told Congress that AI-driven patches were to blame for the service disruptions.

On Thursday, President Trump replaced Sean Cairncross, a top U.S. cybersecurity official, following the string of recent IT outages, including the one that impacted the NSA. Kirsten Davies, a top technology official at the Pentagon, is…
items.t: Behind the recent wave of IT outages: AI is driving an unprecedented number of software patches

items.title: AI could soon be recommending whom to lay off, Arist CEO Michael Ioffe predicts: ‘The speed of decision-making is so much faster’
items.summary:
AI is already fueling workers’ fears of being replaced. Now, one startup CEO predicts it could soon help companies decide whether to lay them off, too.

“We do expect that within the next few years, the majority of significant enterprise shifts, whether it’s products you’re launching, you know, layoffs that you’re making, et cetera, will be recommended by agents,” Michael Ioffe, cofounder and CEO of Arist, said while speaking with Fortune ‘s Kristin Stoller at the Fortune 500 Innovation Forum in Detroit.

Ioffe’s company uses AI agents to interview employees, comb through company data, and recommend solutions to business problems. Arist already works with more than 15% of the Fortune 500, and its technology can gather insights from thousands of employees in just 72 hours—a process that traditionally requires teams of consultants. Still, he doesn’t envision executives handing over control entirely. 

“At the end of the day, it will always be an executive who is making the final call,” Ioffe said. 

That prediction comes as more companies cite AI when cutting jobs, sometimes drawing accusations of “AI washing,” or blaming technology for cuts made for other reasons. But even when companies genuinely expect AI to replace workers, moving too quickly can backfire. As Stoller previously reported , HR leaders have warned that companies risk losing valuable talent when they cut workers without a clear plan for how AI will replace their work.

For Ioffe, the appeal is speed. When sales fall or a product struggles, companies often spend months and millions of dollars working with…
items.t: AI could soon be recommending whom to lay off, Arist CEO Michael Ioffe predicts: ‘The speed of decision-making is so much faster’
